title: Dogen's Genjokoan - at Bozeman Zen Group
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Here's a summary paragraph in plain language: The talk emphasizes the importance of approaching spiritual practice with an open mind and a willingness to let go of attachments and preconceptions. By doing so, we can allow ourselves to be fully present and connected to our experiences, rather than trying to achieve some kind of enlightenment or understanding. This means embracing our true nature as it is, without trying to grasp or control anything, and simply being with what is in the moment.

This piece, Genjokoan, is a really important piece by Dogen.

This piece appears to have started out as a letter to one of his supporters, a lay person in the imperial world somewhere.

Page 24, first paragraph.

He starts off saying:
*As all things are Buddha Dharma, there is delusion, realization, practice, birth and death, Buddhas and sentient beings.
As myriad things are without an abiding self, there is no delusion, no realization, no Buddha, no sentient beings, no birth and death.
The Buddha way in essence, is leaping clear of abundance and lack.
Thus, there is birth and death, delusion and realization, sentient beings and Buddhas.*
We'll stop there.
The next one should be another paragraph, probably.
So here we have some Zen stuff right out of the gate, right?
It is and it isn't, and because it is and isn't, it is and it isn't, and so on and so forth.
It actually is a little challenging even for scholars to work out his exact logic here.
But I think the point is pretty clear, and we talked about this yesterday too.
We have our foot in these two worlds to some extent, more in one than the other usually.
The world of the relative, of the conditioned, of our personalities and problems and ideas and language and concepts, the blurry world of thinking and thinking and worrying and fretting.
But we also sometimes feel the peace of the world, right?
The peace that's behind the words or in between the words and concepts.
Sometimes it's called the absolute or awakening or something like that.
Within these two worlds, we have two kinds of beings, two big groups of beings: broken ordinary people like us, called here sentient beings, and Buddhas.
They seem like very different things.

Naturally, with our foot mostly in the relative world, buffeted by the winds of the world all the time, we believe more in being a broken person, even if sometimes we deny that really well for a long time.
But it's in there.
And a Buddha seems like this impossible aspiration, but maybe practice will help, because nothing else did.
So maybe that's how we start.
But he's saying here it's a mistake to have this division.
There are a lot of ways you could look at it that would be much more helpful, and then the best way to look at it is to jump clear of all those ways of looking at it.
So the key line is towards the end here, where he says, the Buddha way in essence is leaping clear of abundance and lack.
So don't get caught.
He lays out this beautiful theory, and now please forget about it.
So you could say: just practice.
We recognize, in some deep way without thinking about it, because the minute we think about it we know what happens, that we are Buddha.
And we know, through plenty of experience, that we are sentient beings.
But we're not stuck in either position.
So it's leaping clear of categories, is what he's saying.
That's how he starts this whole essay: this, not this; this, not this; this, not this.
Sometimes I think about these teachings, this whole piece.
It isn't a normal essay from our point of view, with an introduction and supporting arguments and a conclusion.
Or maybe each sentence is that whole thing, really condensed.
It's more like a bunch of mental and spiritual yoga working on our mind, putting us into positions that we thought we could never quite do, and stretching our mind.
So maybe that's the way to think about it.
Often what's suggested is: yeah, think about this stuff, sure.
Dogen was very scornful of people who thought, "This doesn't make sense."
He said that very explicitly in another piece.
But don't think about it too much.
Also, let the feeling of it roll over you.

Let the feeling of the words come into your heart and stretch your mind, and if there's any little part in there that pops out at you, like, "Oh," then just let that be a moment of appreciation and joy, and don't try too much to figure it out.

But the conclusion, that thus there is birth and death, delusion, realization, sentient beings and Buddhas, is saying that if you understand the previous part, then you can be in this relative world in a grounded, open way.
Then you can practice, because you know that it's all actually leaping clear of all these categories.
These categories are just ideas and conventions that are designed to help us, skillful means.
Don't get lost in them.
Jump clear.
So that's a challenging bit, but I felt like he opened with it, so it didn't seem legit to skip it.
Then the next one I want to talk about is much more accessible and really cool.
Actually, before that, just this last line of this paragraph is pretty great all by itself, very sensible.
It's not clear how the "yet" attaches, but:
*Yet in attachment, blossoms fall and in aversion, weeds spread.*
So this is a serious everyday life practice suggestion, isn't it?
To notice our attachment and our aversion.
To notice what happens in the mind when we want something, or we want something never to stop or never to leave.
A relationship, a material thing, a great idea you just had that you're worried you're going to forget.
What happens?
Blossoms fall.

What's nice about chanting this, and we chant it in our rituals at home, so you can chant this too, or read it many times, is that it plants the seed that may germinate into a teaching phrase the next time you are really annoyed by impermanence, really upset by it, and justly so.
And what's the thing that we're most attached to?
Life itself, right?
So it's really horrifying when people die, it is.

Well, what are we doing, right?
We're fertilizing the weeds in our mind.
You can probably guess what we're fertilizing them with.

This matches cognitive psychology perfectly, right?
The more you rehearse the thought, the stronger it gets, and the more you believe it and the more bitter and angry you are.
The way you use your mind, what you practice gets stronger, is a great aphorism for all of us.
What you practice gets stronger.
So Dogen, with this one line, is telling us, well, what do you want to practice?
Do you want to practice attachment and be so upset about the falling blossoms?
Do you want to practice aversion and fertilize the weeds?

And so the rest of this essay is about other ways that we can be.
Isn't that nice?
And next time you're upset, see if that'll pop up and maybe it'll help, or maybe it'll just piss you off some more.

What do they know?
Yeah.
At the bottom of this page is Dogen's probably most famous teaching ever.
It's the very beginning of the very last paragraph on page 24 here.
